```{r}
#| label: setup
library(tidyverse)
library(httr2)
library(jsonlite)
library(knitr)

snapshot <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/AnissSahraoui/DATA607/main/Week9/data/"

accent   <- "#2a78d6"
accent_2 <- "#eb6834"
theme_nyt <- theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), plot.title.position = "plot")
```

# The API and the Question

## The endpoint

I used the **Article Search API**
(`https://api.nytimes.com/svc/search/v2/articlesearch.json`). Given a search term and a date range,
it returns article metadata — headline, byline, section, publication date, word count and keywords —
ten articles at a time, along with `meta.hits`, the **total number of matching articles**. That
total is the useful part: it is a complete count, not a sample.

## The question

**How has the Times' coverage of artificial intelligence changed between 2019 and 2026 — both in
volume, and in which sections of the paper carry it?**

The idea is that a subject usually enters a newspaper through a specialist section and, if it
becomes important enough, spreads into general news. If AI has followed that path, it should show
up as a change in the mix of sections, not only in the number of articles.

I compare **January–June 2019** against **January–June 2026**, the same six calendar months seven
years apart, so seasonal differences do not affect the comparison.

# The Request

## Authentication

The key is never written into the code. It lives in my private `~/.Renviron` file as
`NYT_API_KEY`, outside the repository, and is read at run time:

```{r}
#| label: auth
api_key <- Sys.getenv("NYT_API_KEY")

# Report only whether a key was found, never the key itself.
tibble(key_found = nzchar(api_key), key_characters = nchar(api_key))
```

It is passed through `req_url_query()`, so `httr2` handles the URL encoding. One consequence worth
knowing: **printing a request object would display the full URL, including the key**, so this
document never prints `req` — only the response status and the parsed body.

## The parameters

```{r}
#| label: request-code
#| eval: false
# One request: all articles matching a topic in one calendar month.
search_month <- function(topic, year, month, page = 0) {
  start <- as.Date(sprintf("%d-%02d-01", year, month))
  end   <- seq(start, by = "1 month", length.out = 2)[2] - 1

  request("https://api.nytimes.com/svc/search/v2/articlesearch.json") |>
    req_url_query(
      q          = topic,                        # search term
      begin_date = format(start, "%Y%m%d"),      # inclusive start, YYYYMMDD
      end_date   = format(end,   "%Y%m%d"),      # inclusive end
      page       = page,                         # 0-indexed, 10 articles per page
      `api-key`  = api_key
    ) |>
    req_perform()
}
```

| Parameter | Value used | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `q` | `artificial intelligence` | The topic being tracked |
| `begin_date` / `end_date` | One calendar month at a time | Gives an exact monthly count, and spreads the article sample evenly across each period |
| `page` | 0 and 1 | Ten articles per page, so two pages per month |
| `api-key` | from `Sys.getenv()` | Never hard coded |

## A live call

This chunk runs only when a key is available, so the document still renders for anyone without one.
It prints the status and the hit count, and nothing that could leak the key.

```{r}
#| label: live-call
#| eval: !expr nzchar(Sys.getenv("NYT_API_KEY"))
resp <- request("https://api.nytimes.com/svc/search/v2/articlesearch.json") |>
  req_url_query(q = "artificial intelligence",
                begin_date = "20260601", end_date = "20260630",
                `api-key` = api_key) |>
  req_error(is_error = \(r) FALSE) |>
  req_perform()

parsed <- resp_body_json(resp)

tibble(
  status         = resp_status(resp),
  total_hits     = parsed$response$meta$hits,
  articles_on_page = length(parsed$response$docs)
)
```

Two practical notes from building this. The API is rate limited to roughly **five requests per
minute**, so the collection script pauses 13 seconds between calls. And the `facet_fields` and `fq`
parameters, which would have returned section counts directly, **return nothing on this access
tier** — every `fq` filter I tried came back with zero hits — so the section breakdown is built from
the returned articles instead.

# From Nested JSON to a Tidy Data Frame

## What the response looks like

The JSON is deeply nested. A single article holds the headline inside a `headline` object, the
author inside a `byline` object, and a variable-length list of keyword objects:

```{r}
#| label: nested-structure
#| eval: !expr nzchar(Sys.getenv("NYT_API_KEY"))
doc <- parsed$response$docs[[1]]

tibble(
  field = c("headline", "byline", "keywords", "section_name"),
  shape = c(
    paste("object with:", paste(names(doc$headline), collapse = ", ")),
    paste("object with:", paste(names(doc$byline), collapse = ", ")),
    paste("list of", length(doc$keywords), "objects, each with name/value"),
    "plain string"
  )
)
```

## The flattening code

Each nested piece is pulled into its own column. `%||%` substitutes `NA` when a field is absent,
which matters because not every article has every field.

```{r}
#| label: flatten-code
#| eval: false
articles <- map_dfr(response$docs, \(d) tibble(
  headline         = d$headline$main    %||% NA_character_,  # unnest object
  byline           = d$byline$original  %||% NA_character_,  # unnest object
  section_name     = d$section_name     %||% NA_character_,
  subsection_name  = d$subsection_name  %||% NA_character_,
  news_desk        = d$news_desk        %||% NA_character_,
  type_of_material = d$type_of_material %||% NA_character_,
  pub_date         = d$pub_date         %||% NA_character_,
  word_count       = d$word_count       %||% NA_integer_,
  n_keywords       = length(d$keywords),                     # list -> count
  keywords         = paste(map_chr(d$keywords, \(k) k$value %||% NA_character_),
                           collapse = "; "),                 # list -> one string
  web_url          = d$web_url          %||% NA_character_
))
```

The full collection script is
[`fetch_nyt.R`](https://github.com/AnissSahraoui/DATA607/blob/main/Week9/fetch_nyt.R).

## The saved snapshot

Nobody without an API key can repeat the collection, and the live totals change daily as the Times
publishes. The script therefore saves its results to CSV, and the analysis below reads those files
from GitHub so the figures in this report stay fixed.

```{r}
#| label: load-snapshot
articles <- read_csv(paste0(snapshot, "nyt_ai_articles.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
monthly  <- read_csv(paste0(snapshot, "nyt_ai_monthly_totals.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)

glimpse(articles)
```

```{r}
#| label: show-articles
articles |>
  select(headline, section_name, type_of_material, pub_date, word_count, n_keywords) |>
  slice_head(n = 5)
```

# Data-Cleaning Decisions

```{r}
#| label: missing
articles |>
  summarise(across(everything(), ~ sum(is.na(.)))) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "column", values_to = "missing") |>
  filter(missing > 0) |>
  kable()
```

Three decisions, each kept rather than silently patched:

- **`subsection_name` is missing for `r sum(is.na(articles$subsection_name))` of
  `r nrow(articles)` articles.** Most articles simply have no subsection, so the blank is
  meaningful. I left it as `NA` and did not use it in the analysis.
- **`byline` is missing for `r sum(is.na(articles$byline))` articles, all from 2019.** These are
  wire copy and briefing items that carry no author. I kept the rows, because the question is about
  sections rather than authors, and dropping them would quietly shrink the 2019 sample.
- **`keywords` is empty for `r sum(is.na(articles$keywords))` articles.** The keyword list is
  flattened into one semicolon-separated string with a count alongside it, so an article with no
  keywords reads as `NA` with `n_keywords` of 0 rather than as an empty string.

```{r}
#| label: integrity
articles |>
  summarise(
    rows              = n(),
    duplicate_urls    = sum(duplicated(web_url)),
    articles_per_year = n_distinct(query_year),
    sections          = n_distinct(section_name),
    date_parses       = sum(!is.na(as.Date(substr(pub_date, 1, 10))))
  ) |>
  kable()
```

No article appears twice, and every publication date parses.

**The sampling decision, which matters most.** The monthly totals are **exact**: they come from
`meta.hits`, which counts every matching article. The section breakdown is a **sample**: 20
articles per month, 120 per period, drawn evenly across the six months so no single month dominates.
The API returns articles in relevance order, so this is the 20 articles it ranked most relevant each
month, not a random draw. I therefore treat the section percentages as indicative rather than exact,
and lean on the shape of the differences rather than on individual percentage points.

# Results

## Volume

```{r}
#| label: volume
period_totals <- monthly |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarise(articles = sum(total_hits), .groups = "drop")

period_totals |> kable(col.names = c("Period (Jan–Jun)", "Articles mentioning AI"))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-monthly
#| fig-cap: "Articles mentioning artificial intelligence, by month. Counts are exact, taken from the API's hit totals."
#| fig-height: 3.4
monthly |>
  mutate(month_name = factor(month.abb[month], levels = month.abb[1:6]),
         year = factor(year)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = month_name, y = total_hits, fill = year)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.75), width = 0.65) +
  geom_text(aes(label = total_hits), position = position_dodge(width = 0.75),
            vjust = -0.4, size = 3.2) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("2019" = accent_2, "2026" = accent), name = NULL) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.12))) +
  labs(title = "AI coverage is more than five times its 2019 level",
       x = NULL, y = "Articles") +
  theme_nyt +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

```{r}
#| label: ratio
ratio <- period_totals$articles[period_totals$year == 2026] /
         period_totals$articles[period_totals$year == 2019]
```

The Times published **`r period_totals$articles[period_totals$year == 2019]`** articles mentioning
AI in the first half of 2019 and **`r period_totals$articles[period_totals$year == 2026]`** in the
same months of 2026, a **`r round(ratio, 1)`-fold increase**. Every month of 2026 exceeds the whole
of any month in 2019.

## Which sections

```{r}
#| label: sections
section_mix <- articles |>
  count(query_year, section_name) |>
  group_by(query_year) |>
  mutate(share = 100 * n / sum(n)) |>
  ungroup()

comparison <- section_mix |>
  select(query_year, section_name, share) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = query_year, values_from = share, names_prefix = "y") |>
  replace_na(list(y2019 = 0, y2026 = 0)) |>
  mutate(change = y2026 - y2019) |>
  arrange(desc(abs(change)))

comparison |>
  slice_head(n = 8) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 1))) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Section", "2019 (%)", "2026 (%)", "Change (pp)"))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-sections
#| fig-cap: "Share of sampled AI articles by section. Only sections reaching 3% in either period are shown."
#| fig-height: 4
section_mix |>
  group_by(section_name) |>
  filter(max(share) >= 3) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(year = factor(query_year),
         section_name = fct_reorder(section_name, share, .fun = max)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = share, y = section_name, fill = year)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.75), width = 0.65) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.1f%%", share)),
            position = position_dodge(width = 0.75), hjust = -0.15, size = 3) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("2019" = accent_2, "2026" = accent), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))) +
  labs(title = "Technology still leads, but AI has moved into general news",
       x = "Share of sampled articles (%)", y = NULL) +
  theme_nyt +
  theme(legend.position = "top", panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())
```

## How concentrated is the coverage?

```{r}
#| label: concentration
section_mix |>
  group_by(query_year) |>
  summarise(
    sections_used  = n_distinct(section_name),
    top_3_share    = round(sum(sort(share, decreasing = TRUE)[1:3]), 1),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Period", "Distinct sections", "Share in top 3 sections (%)"))
```

```{r}
#| label: material
articles |>
  mutate(commentary = type_of_material %in% c("Op-Ed", "Editorial", "Letter")) |>
  group_by(query_year) |>
  summarise(
    commentary_share = round(100 * mean(commentary), 1),
    median_words     = median(word_count),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Period", "Commentary (%)", "Median word count"))
```

# Conclusions

- **Volume has grown more than fivefold.** AI went from
  `r period_totals$articles[period_totals$year == 2019]` articles in the first half of 2019 to
  `r period_totals$articles[period_totals$year == 2026]` in the same months of 2026. This figure is
  exact rather than sampled, since it comes from the API's own hit counts.
- **Technology remains the home section, and that has not changed.** It accounts for about 30% of
  sampled AI articles in both periods, with Business around 21–23%. The subject did not migrate
  away from the technology desk; the rest of the paper joined in.
- **The clearest shift is from commentary to news.** Opinion fell from
  `r round(comparison$y2019[comparison$section_name == "Opinion"], 1)`% of sampled articles to
  `r round(comparison$y2026[comparison$section_name == "Opinion"], 1)`%, while the U.S. section rose
  from `r round(comparison$y2019[comparison$section_name == "U.S."], 1)`% to
  `r round(comparison$y2026[comparison$section_name == "U.S."], 1)`% and New York went from nothing
  to `r round(comparison$y2026[comparison$section_name == "New York"], 1)`%. Counting by article
  type rather than section says the same thing: commentary pieces fell from 20.8% to 6.7% of the
  sample.
- **Coverage has spread out.** The top three sections held 74.2% of sampled AI articles in 2019 and
  64.2% in 2026.
- **Read together, this looks like a subject becoming a beat.** In 2019 AI was something the paper
  argued *about*, in Opinion and in Technology. By 2026 it is something reported *on* — in national
  news, in local New York coverage, and even in Real Estate and Theater. The articles are also
  slightly shorter, with the median falling from 1,100 to 933 words, which fits routine news
  reporting rather than occasional long essays.

**What would strengthen this.** The section percentages rest on 120 articles per period chosen by
the API's relevance ranking, not a random sample. With a higher access tier the `facet_fields`
parameter would return exact section counts, and the same comparison could then be made on complete
data rather than on a sample. The hit totals, which carry the headline finding, do not have this
limitation.
